root_cause.text: KVM’s SVM `invlpga_interception()` handler did not check whether `EFER.SVME` was enabled before emulating `INVLPGA`, so the guest instruction was handled instead of causing the architecturally required `#UD` when SVM was disabled.
root_cause.evidence: The patch adds `if (nested_svm_check_permissions(vcpu)) return 1;` at the start of `arch/x86/kvm/svm/svm.c::invlpga_interception()`, and the commit message explicitly says `INVLPGA should cause a #UD when EFER.SVME is not set` and that this adds the missing check for `EFER.SVME=0`.

intent_record.intent_summary: Add an early nested SVM permission check to block invalid INVLPGA handling when nested virtualization disallows the operation.
intent_record.what: A call to nested_svm_check_permissions(vcpu) was inserted at the start of invlpga_interception(), and if it returns true the function now exits early with return 1 before any further INVLPGA handling.
intent_record.how: At runtime, this causes nested SVM permission validation to run before processing the intercepted INVLPGA instruction, preventing the rest of the handler from executing when nested virtualization permissions disallow it.

grouping_result.intent: Add an early nested SVM permission check to block invalid INVLPGA handling when nested virtualization disallows the operation.

relevance_review.reason: The change adds an early SVM permission check before handling INVLPGA, which aligns with the root cause of missing validation before emulating INVLPGA when SVM is disabled and #UD should be raised.

candidates.rationale: This is the start of INVLPGA emulation in the interception handler. In the vulnerable code path, the handler proceeded to emulate the instruction based on guest registers without first checking whether SVM was enabled, so execution reached this point instead of raising #UD.

This line is part of the same unchecked emulation path, reading guest state to perform INVLPGA handling. Because no EFER.SVME validation occurred before using these operands, the handler could incorrectly emulate the instruction when it should have faulted.
